newsitem.title: USA: Atheist challenges South Carolina's "God clause".
newsitem.headline: Atheist challenges South Carolina's "God clause".

text.p: The lawyer for a South Carolina atheist told state Supreme Court judges on Thursday that his client was discriminated against when his application to become a notary public was rejected because of his beliefs.
The Supreme Court hearing was Herb Silverman's latest challenge of a state constitutional requirement that public officers acknowledge a "supreme" being.
Silverman, a 54-year-old College of Charleston math teacher, filed the application in 1992, and has spent the last six years fighting for atheist rights in the Bible Belt state.

"Of 30,000 applications for notary public, this is the only one that is from a devout atheist and the only one that has been denied," Silverman's ACLU appointed lawyer, Edmund Robinson, told the court's five justices.

But the state's lawyer, Brad Waring, said constitutional officers rejected Silverman's application only because it lacked the correct number of signatures and he had crossed out the word "God" from the constitutionally-required oath.

"If the word protect, preserve or defend had been struck from the application, the result would have been exactly the same," Waring said. "There was no religious discrimination in this case, and there was no evidence presented of it."
Robinson told the justices the case now "cries out for a court ruling on the merits of the constitutional controversy." The justices gave no indication when they might rule.

The case wound up in the state Supreme Court after Republican Gov. David Beasley, a born-again Christian, appealed a lower court ruling that South Carolina had violated the First Amendment by barring atheists from public office.

"The state cannot require any religious belief including a call for 'God's help' as a requirement for appointment to office," Circuit Judge Thomas Hughston Jr. wrote in his ruling, referring to the notary public's pledge to fulfil duties "so help me God."
South Carolina's Constitution since 1868 has said: "No person who denies the existence of the Supreme Being shall hold any office under this Constitution."
Silverman, who is on sabbatical in California and was not present in court Thursday, first challenged the "God clause" when he ran for governor as a write-in candidate in 1990.

"I am qualified to be a professor of mathematics at a state institution, but I don't have the morals to be a notary public because I happen to not believe in a Supreme Being," he later complained in an interview.
Six other states -- North Carolina, Texas, Tennessee, Arkansas, Maryland and Pennsylvania -- have a similar clause, but do not enforce it.
